Record *raw data*, the numbers as the instrument gave them, and never overwrite them. Do calculations in separate columns later. A smudged, corrected or 'improved' raw number is worthless, because no one, including you, can tell what was actually observed. Scientists keep bound notebooks with numbered pages for exactly this reason.

Write down everything unusual. A pot got knocked over; the room was unusually warm on day 9; the microscope lamp flickered. When a strange value, an *outlier*, appears in the data, the notes tell you whether it came from a real event or from a known accident. Throwing out an outlier because it spoils the pattern is not allowed. Throwing it out because the notes say the sample was contaminated, and saying so in the report, is good practice.

If you use this site's microscope for a project, the same rules apply: note the magnification, the stain, the time since the slide was made and the field of view you counted. Two counts of cells in a drop of pond water made under different conditions are not the same measurement, and the notes are what let you tell the difference.

words.d: checking an instrument against a known standard so its readings can be trusted
the smallest change in a quantity that an instrument can show
measurements recorded exactly as the instrument gave them, before any calculation or correction
a data value far from the rest, which may be a real event or a known error

look.title: The Value That Spoils the Graph
look.text: Nine readings of a reaction time cluster between 0.21 and 0.26 seconds. The tenth is 0.91 seconds. A student wants to delete it because it ruins the average. Her notes for that trial say: 'phone buzzed on the desk right before the light came on.'
look.prompt: Should the tenth value be removed? What would justify removing it, and what should the report say either way?

check.q: A thermometer placed in an ice-water bath reads 2 degrees Celsius. What has the student learned?
choices: The ice is too warm
Ice-water baths are unreliable
The thermometer has a systematic offset that must be corrected or the thermometer replaced
The thermometer has high resolution
check.why: An ice-water bath is a known standard at 0 degrees Celsius; a reading of 2 degrees shows a calibration error.

check.q: Why should raw data never be overwritten with corrected values?
choices: Because erasers are expensive
Because corrected values are always wrong
Because the notebook must be handed in unchanged
Because no one can then tell what was actually observed
check.why: Raw data are the only record of the observation itself; corrections belong in separate columns where they can be checked.

check.q: When is it acceptable to exclude an outlier from analysis?
choices: When notes show a known error in that trial, and the exclusion is reported
Whenever it spoils the pattern
When the average would otherwise be too high
Never, under any circumstances
check.why: Exclusion is justified only by a documented problem with the measurement, and it must be stated in the report.

lessons.title: Finding the Pattern
lessons.mainIdea: Analysis means summarizing the data, plotting them and asking whether the pattern is bigger than the scatter.
reading: With the data in hand, the first step is to summarize each group. The *mean*, the sum divided by the count, is the everyday average. The *median*, the middle value when the data are sorted, is better when a few extreme values would drag the mean around. The *range*, or a more careful measure of spread like the standard deviation, tells you how scattered the values are. Report both a center and a spread; a mean without a spread is a claim without an uncertainty.

Next, plot the data. Put the independent variable on the horizontal axis and the dependent variable on the vertical, with every point shown, not just the averages. A picture reveals what a table hides: whether the relationship is a straight line, a curve that flattens out, or no relationship at all. If the points fall roughly along a line, a *best-fit line* drawn through them gives a rate, and its slope has units, such as centimeters of growth per hour of light per day.

The key question is whether the pattern is larger than the noise. If the 12-hour seedlings average 14 centimeters and the 4-hour seedlings average 12, but each group's values range from 9 to 17, the difference is inside the scatter and you have not shown anything. If the ranges barely overlap, the difference is real. Statistical tests put a number on this: how often would chance alone produce a difference this big? A result that chance would produce fewer than 1 time in 20 is usually called significant, but that is a convention, not a law of nature, and a tiny significant difference may not matter.

Beware of the pattern that fits too well. With enough freedom you can draw a wiggly curve through any set of points, and it will predict nothing. Prefer the simplest relationship that fits the data within its uncertainty, and check whether it fits new data you did not use to draw it.

words.d: the sum of the values divided by how many there are; the ordinary average
the middle value when the data are sorted; less affected by extreme values than the mean
the difference between the largest and smallest values, a simple measure of spread
a straight line drawn through plotted data so that it passes as close as possible to all the points

look.title: A Pendulum's Length and Its Swing
look.cite: Standard physics, period = 2 pi times the square root of length divided by g, with g = 9.8 m/s squared, rounded
look.prompt: Doubling the length does not double the period. Plot the points in your head: is the pattern a straight line? What happens to the period when the length is multiplied by four?

check.q: Reaction times for a class are mostly near 0.25 seconds, but two students scored 1.5 seconds. Which summary best represents a typical student?
choices: The mean
The median
The largest value
The sum
check.why: The median ignores how extreme the outliers are, while the two slow times would pull the mean well above what most students scored.

check.q: Two groups have means of 14 cm and 12 cm, but values in each group range from 9 to 17 cm. What can be concluded?
choices: The treatment clearly works
The 12 cm group was measured wrong
The difference is within the scatter, so no effect has been shown
The experiment should be published
check.why: A difference smaller than the spread within groups could easily arise by chance; more data or a larger effect would be needed.

check.q: Why prefer the simplest curve that fits the data over a wiggly one that passes through every point?
choices: Simple curves are easier to draw
Wiggly curves use too much ink
Teachers prefer straight lines
A curve that fits every wiggle is fitting noise and will not predict new data
check.why: Overfitting captures random scatter rather than the real relationship; a simpler fit generalizes better and can be tested on new data.

lessons.title: Models and Their Limits
lessons.mainIdea: A model is a deliberate simplification that lets you predict and explain, and it is only as trustworthy as its record against real data.
reading: A *model* is a stand-in for something too big, too small, too slow or too complicated to work with directly. A globe is a model of Earth. An equation relating a pendulum's length to its period is a mathematical model. A computer *simulation* of the atmosphere, dividing the air into millions of boxes and stepping their temperature and wind forward in time, is a model too. Every one of them leaves things out on purpose. The globe has no weather; the pendulum equation ignores air resistance; the climate model cannot track every cloud.

The leaving-out is the point, and it is also the danger. Each model rests on *assumptions*, and it is only reliable where those assumptions hold. The pendulum equation works beautifully for small swings and fails for wide ones. The bead-on-a-string picture of genes that McClintock's colleagues held was a useful model that made good predictions for decades, right up until her corn showed genes moving. A model that has never been wrong may just never have been tested outside its comfortable range.

So the test of a model is its record. Does it predict measurements it was not built from? Where does it start to fail, and does the failure make sense? Weather models are checked every single day against what actually happened, which is why a five-day forecast today is about as good as a three-day forecast was decades ago. When a model and a careful measurement disagree, the measurement usually wins, and the disagreement is where the next discovery hides.

For your own project you will build at least a simple model: a line through data points, a diagram of a food web, a formula relating your variables. State its assumptions. Say where you expect it to hold and where you do not. A reader who sees that you know the limits of your model will trust the parts inside them.

words.d: a simplified representation of a system, physical, mathematical or computer-based, used to explain and predict
a computer model that calculates how a system changes step by step over time
something a model takes as true in order to simplify, which limits where the model applies

look.title: Wrong but Useful
look.text: The statistician George Box argued that since every model simplifies, every model is in some sense wrong, and the useful question is not whether a model is exactly true but whether it is good enough to help with the problem at hand. Some models, he said, are useful in spite of being wrong.
look.cite: George E. P. Box, paper on science and statistics, 1976 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: If every model is wrong, how can a scientist decide which one to use? What kind of evidence would tell you a model is good enough for a particular question?

check.q: The pendulum equation ignores air resistance. Why is that acceptable?
choices: It is a deliberate simplification that works well within the range where air resistance is small
Air resistance does not exist for pendulums
Equations are not allowed to include air
Because the model has never been tested
check.why: Models leave things out on purpose; the omission is fine as long as you know where it makes the model fail.

check.q: What is the best test of whether a model can be trusted?
choices: Whether it is written by a famous scientist
Whether it correctly predicts measurements it was not built from
Whether it includes every detail of the system
Whether it uses a computer
check.why: A model earns trust by its record against new data; the more detailed a model is, the harder it is to check, not the more correct.

check.q: McClintock's colleagues used a model of genes as fixed beads on a string. What does her story show about models?
choices: Models should never be used in genetics
Old models are always replaced by better ones every decade
A model that works well for a long time can still fail when tested in a new situation
Models are only useful in physics
check.why: The bead model made good predictions until data outside its range appeared; that is how models are corrected.

lessons.title: Criteria and Constraints
lessons.mainIdea: An engineering problem is defined by measurable criteria for success and firm constraints that any solution must obey.
reading: Science asks what is true; engineering asks what will work. A school wants to cut the flooding on its playing field after storms. Before anyone sketches a solution, the problem needs a sharp definition. The *criteria* are what a successful design must do, written so that they can be measured: standing water gone within 12 hours of a 2-centimeter rain; no damage to the running track; safe for students. Vague criteria like 'better drainage' cannot be tested and cannot settle an argument between two designs.

The *constraints* are the limits every design must stay inside: a budget of a certain amount, a completion date before the fall season, no digging near the buried gas line, compliance with the city's stormwater rules. A design that fails a constraint is out, no matter how well it scores on the criteria. Listing constraints early saves everyone from falling in love with a design that could never be built.

Almost no design wins on every criterion, so engineers face *trade-offs*. A deep gravel trench drains fastest but costs the most and takes longest to build. A raised field is cheap but changes the playing surface. A *decision matrix* makes the trade-offs visible: list the designs as rows and the criteria as columns, score each cell, weight the criteria by how much they matter, and add up. The matrix does not decide for you, but it forces you to say out loud which criteria you value most and why.

This is the same claim, evidence and reasoning habit in a new dress. The claim is that a design meets the criteria within the constraints; the evidence is test data and cost figures; the reasoning shows how the trade-offs were weighed. Notice that criteria and constraints usually come from people, not from nature, and that different stakeholders, the coach, the neighbors, the budget office, will weight them differently.

words.d: the measurable requirements a successful design must meet
the limits, such as cost, time, materials, safety or law, that any design must stay within
giving up some of one desirable feature to gain more of another
a table that scores each design against each criterion to make comparisons and trade-offs visible

look.title: Two Bridges for the Creek
look.text: A park district needs a footbridge over a creek. Design A is steel, costs the whole budget, lasts 75 years and can be installed in a week. Design B is treated wood, costs half the budget, lasts about 25 years and needs three weeks of work. The constraints are the budget and finishing before the summer camp opens in four weeks. Criteria: safety, lifespan, cost, appearance.
look.prompt: Both designs meet the constraints. Build a decision matrix in your head with weights. Which criterion would have to matter most for each design to win?

check.q: Which of these is a constraint rather than a criterion?
choices: The field should drain within 12 hours
The design should not harm the running track
Students should be able to use the field safely
The project must cost no more than the approved budget
check.why: A constraint is a hard limit any design must obey; the others describe what a successful design should accomplish.

check.q: Why must criteria be written so they can be measured?
choices: So that designs can be compared and disagreements settled with evidence
Because engineers like numbers
So that the project can be finished faster
Because unmeasured criteria are illegal
check.why: Only measurable criteria allow a test to show whether a design succeeded, which is how evidence rather than opinion decides.

check.q: What does a decision matrix actually do?
choices: It chooses the best design automatically
It makes the scores and the weights on each criterion visible so trade-offs can be discussed
It replaces the need for testing
It removes all constraints
check.why: The matrix organizes judgments and forces the weighting of criteria into the open; people still make the decision.

lessons.title: Build, Test, Fail, Improve
lessons.mainIdea: Designs improve through cycles of building a prototype, testing it against the criteria, studying the failures and trying again.
reading: Engineering rarely gets a design right the first time, and it does not expect to. The design cycle runs: define the problem, brainstorm, build a *prototype*, test it, study what went wrong, revise, and test again. A prototype is a working version made quickly and cheaply enough that you are willing to break it. A cardboard model of the drainage trench, a scale bridge made of craft sticks, a spreadsheet of the costs: each is a prototype of a different part of the design.

The test must be against the written criteria, not against a feeling that it looks good. Load the craft-stick bridge with weights until it breaks and record the mass. Pour a measured amount of water on the model field and time how long it stands. Comparing prototypes on the same test is what turns opinion into evidence. Numbers from a fair test also settle arguments between team members far more peacefully than volume does.

The most valuable step is *failure analysis*: figuring out why a prototype failed rather than just that it did. Did the bridge break at a joint or in the middle of a stick? Did the water pool because the slope was wrong or because the gravel clogged? In 1901 the Wright brothers found that the published tables of lift they had trusted were wrong, built their own wind tunnel, and tested more than a hundred wing shapes before the 1903 flight. In 1940 the Tacoma Narrows Bridge twisted itself apart in a moderate wind, and the study of that failure changed how every long bridge since has been designed.

Each cycle is an *iteration*, and the number of iterations is not a sign of poor work. Commercial products often go through hundreds or thousands of prototypes. The record of what was tried, what failed and why is as important as the final design, because the next engineer, or you next year, will need it.

words.d: an early, quick version of a design built to be tested and probably broken
the study of exactly how and why a design failed, to guide the next version
one complete cycle of building, testing and revising a design

look.title: The Bridge That Held 4 Kilograms
look.text: A team's craft-stick bridge is required to span 40 centimeters and hold 5 kilograms. Their first prototype holds 4 kilograms and then snaps where two sticks are glued end to end near the middle of the span. A teammate says: 'Just use more glue everywhere.'
look.prompt: What does the failure tell you about where the bridge is weak? Propose a specific change for the next iteration and say how you would test whether it worked.

check.q: What is the purpose of a prototype?
choices: To be the final product sold to customers
To avoid having to test the design
To test a design cheaply enough that breaking it is acceptable
To impress the client
check.why: A prototype is built to be tested and often broken, so that failures are found while they are still cheap.

check.q: Why did the Wright brothers build their own wind tunnel?
choices: Because wind tunnels were fashionable
To sell it to other inventors
Because they had no place to fly
Because the published lift data they had relied on turned out to be wrong
check.why: When their gliders underperformed, they traced the failure to bad published data and generated their own through systematic testing.

check.q: Which is the best response to a prototype bridge breaking at a glued joint?
choices: Analyze why the joint failed and redesign that joint for the next iteration
Add more glue everywhere and hope
Abandon the project
Declare the test unfair
check.why: Failure analysis targets the actual weak point; a blanket fix wastes effort and may not address the cause.

lessons.title: Writing a Scientific Explanation
lessons.mainIdea: A written explanation states the claim, presents the evidence with numbers and uncertainty, reasons from principle, and admits what it cannot rule out.
reading: The claim comes first, in one sentence, answering the question you asked. 'Bean seedlings given 12 hours of daily light grew taller over 21 days than seedlings given 4 hours.' Not 'light affects plants,' which is too vague to test, and not 'light is essential to all life,' which your data cannot support. State it in the past tense about what you found, and keep it inside the range you tested.

The evidence follows, with numbers. Means with their spread, the number of subjects, and a graph or table the reader can inspect. 'The 12-hour group averaged 14.2 centimeters, ranging 12.5 to 16.0, across 10 seedlings; the 4-hour group averaged 9.8 centimeters, ranging 8.1 to 11.4.' Then the reasoning: the scientific principle that explains why this evidence supports the claim, such as light supplying the energy for photosynthesis, which builds the sugars used for growth. Reasoning is where you connect your small experiment to what is already known.

The strongest explanations then turn on themselves. Name the *alternative explanations* you considered and say what evidence rules them out: could the 12-hour lamp also have warmed the pots? If you measured temperature and it was the same, say so; if you did not, say that too. State the *limitations*: one bean variety, three weeks, indoor conditions. A reader who sees you searching for your own weaknesses is a reader who begins to trust you.

Finally, give credit. A *citation* for every fact, value or method that came from someone else tells the reader where to check and shows that you built on real work rather than invention. McClintock's papers were dense with cross-references to decades of maize genetics, which is part of why they held up when they were finally read carefully.

words.d: a different cause that could also account for the evidence, which a good explanation tries to rule out
a boundary on what a study can show, such as its sample, duration or conditions
a reference that tells the reader where a fact, method or value came from

look.title: Knowing You Are Right
look.text: Late in her life McClintock reflected that when the response to her jumping genes was disbelief, she did not feel discouraged. She said that if you know you are on the right track and have that inner certainty from the evidence, no one can turn you away from it, whatever they say. She also said that she had simply kept working, because the corn kept confirming the result season after season.
look.cite: Barbara McClintock, remarks and interviews around the time of her 1983 Nobel Prize (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Inner certainty is also what people feel about ideas that are wrong. What separated McClintock's certainty from mere stubbornness, and how would that show up in a written explanation?

check.q: Which claim stays properly inside the range of the seedling experiment?
choices: Light is essential to all life on Earth
Seedlings given 12 hours of daily light grew taller over 21 days than those given 4 hours
Plants should always get 12 hours of light
Light affects plants
check.why: A claim should state what was found under the tested conditions, neither too vague nor broader than the data.

check.q: Why should a written explanation name alternative explanations?
choices: To make the report longer
Because reviewers require a fixed number of them
To show that other causes were considered and, where possible, ruled out by evidence
To confuse the reader
check.why: Considering and testing alternatives is how an explanation earns trust; leaving them out invites the reader to find them.

check.q: What does a citation accomplish?
choices: It makes the writing look academic
It proves the claim is true
It replaces the need for evidence
It tells the reader where a fact or method came from so it can be checked
check.why: Citations give credit and, more importantly, let readers trace and verify what the explanation rests on.

lessons.title: Presenting and Defending a Claim
lessons.mainIdea: Defending a claim means answering objections with evidence, separating questions of fact from questions of value, and changing your mind when the evidence demands it.
reading: A scientific presentation, whether a talk, a poster or a written report, is an argument, and arguments draw fire. Prepare for it. Before you present, list the five hardest questions someone could ask and work out your answers. Most objections come in a few forms: your sample was too small, you did not control something, there is a simpler explanation, or your numbers do not show what you say they show. Each of these is a *counterclaim*, and each deserves a *rebuttal* that points at evidence, not at your effort or your confidence.

Some objections will be right. The honest response to a good objection is to say so, and to say what you would do about it: 'That is a fair point; we did not measure temperature, and the lamp could have warmed the pots. The next run should include a thermometer in each pot.' Scientists who cannot say 'you are right' in public are not trusted in private either. The goal of a defense is not to win but to find out, together with your critics, what the evidence actually supports.

Learn to separate two kinds of disagreement. Whether CFCs destroy ozone is a question of fact, settled by measurement. Whether the cost of phasing them out was worth it is a question of values, on which measurement informs but does not decide. In a *poster session* or a public meeting, people mix the two constantly. Naming which kind of question is on the table is often the most useful thing a presenter can do.

Two cautionary tales frame the skill. The cold fusion scientists of 1989 were confident, presented dramatically and were wrong. McClintock was quiet, thorough and right, but her audience was not ready and she stopped pushing. The lesson is not that confidence is bad or that being ignored proves you correct. It is that a claim stands or falls on the evidence and on how carefully it was gathered, and the presenter's job is to make that evidence as clear and as checkable as possible.

words.d: an opposing claim or objection raised against an argument
a response to an objection that uses evidence and reasoning to answer it
a scientific meeting format in which researchers stand beside a printed summary of their work and answer questions

look.title: Questions From the Back Row
look.text: A student presents a project showing that a wetland at the edge of town lowered nitrate levels in a creek. A listener asks: 'How do you know the drop was not just because it rained less that month?' Another says: 'Even if it works, that land should be used for housing.'
look.prompt: Which question is about fact and which is about values? Write the strongest rebuttal to the first one, and say what data would be needed if the student does not have them.

check.q: A critic says your control group was not treated identically. What is the best response?
choices: Explain what evidence shows the groups were matched, or admit the gap and say how you would fix it
Say that you worked very hard on the project
Point out that the critic's own work has flaws
Ignore the question and move on
check.why: A rebuttal rests on evidence; where the objection is valid, conceding it and proposing a fix is the honest and trusted response.

check.q: Which is a question of values rather than of fact?
choices: Does the wetland lower nitrate levels in the creek?
Should the town keep the wetland instead of building houses on it?
How much did rainfall change during the study?
What is the nitrate concentration upstream?
check.why: Whether to keep the wetland depends on what people value; the other questions can be settled by measurement.

check.q: What lesson do the cold fusion and McClintock stories teach together?
choices: Confident presenters are usually wrong
Ignored scientists are usually right
A claim stands on the quality of its evidence, not on the manner of the presenter
Press conferences are the best way to announce results
check.why: One confident claim failed and one quiet claim succeeded because of the evidence behind each, not the presentation style.

lessons.title: Your Capstone Plan
lessons.mainIdea: A capstone plan lays out the question, the design, the data, the analysis, the safety steps and the timeline before any measurement is made.
reading: Your *capstone* project is one investigation, chosen by you, carried through every stage this unit has covered. It can be an experiment, a field study, an analysis of existing data or an engineering design, but it must produce evidence and end with a defended claim. Start with what you are curious about near you: the temperature of Chicago's lakefront versus an inland neighborhood, the number of organisms in a drop of pond water under this site's microscope, the craters visible on the moon with its telescope on different nights, the drainage on your own school's field. Local questions are easier to measure and harder to fake.

The written plan has a fixed set of parts. The testable question and hypothesis. Background: what is already known, with citations. The variables, identifying which is independent, which dependent and which controlled, or the criteria and constraints if it is a design. The protocol, step by step, with materials. The data table, empty, with units. The analysis plan: what you will calculate and what graph you will draw. Safety and ethics. And a line stating what result would make you abandon the hypothesis.

Then the *timeline*. Work backward from the presentation date and set *milestones*: plan approved, pilot run done, data collection finished, analysis done, draft written, practice defense. Plants take weeks to grow and pond water changes with the seasons, so the calendar is a real constraint. Build in slack, because a pilot will reveal something that needs changing.

Everything in the plan is a promise to your future self and to your readers about how the work will be done, made before the results can tempt you to bend it. That is preregistration in miniature, and it is the single best protection against fooling yourself. When the data come in, you will analyze them the way you said you would, report what you find whether or not it is what you hoped, and stand up to defend it. That is the whole practice of science in one project.

words.d: a final project that brings together every skill of a course in one complete investigation
a schedule that sets when each stage of a project will be done
a checkpoint in a project where a specific piece of work must be complete

look.title: Two Weeks Before the Deadline
look.text: A student's capstone plan says she will compare how many pond organisms appear in samples from a shaded pond edge and a sunny pond edge, counting under the microscope at the same magnification, five samples from each, over three visits. It is now two weeks before the presentation, the first visit is done and it rained hard yesterday.
look.prompt: What should her timeline include for the next two weeks, and what should she write in her notes about the rain? What could she do if the counts cannot be finished?

check.q: Why does the plan include a statement of what result would make you abandon the hypothesis?
choices: To make the plan longer
Because teachers require it
Because every hypothesis is eventually abandoned
So that the decision is made before the results can tempt you to bend the analysis
check.why: Deciding in advance what would count against the hypothesis is preregistration in miniature and protects against fooling yourself.

check.q: Which of these is a milestone?
choices: Data collection finished by October 15
The hypothesis
The dependent variable
The list of citations
check.why: A milestone is a dated checkpoint for a piece of work; the other items are parts of the plan, not points on the timeline.

check.q: Why does the reading recommend local questions for a capstone?
choices: Because distant places are not scientific
Because they are easier to measure directly and harder to fake
Because Illinois has more science than other states
Because local questions are always simpler
check.why: Local phenomena can be measured firsthand with available tools, which makes the evidence real and checkable.

review.q: Which question is testable as written?
choices: Is pollution bad?
Why is nature amazing?
Does the mass of a craft-stick bridge affect the load it holds before breaking, for spans of 40 centimeters?
Are bridges important?
review.why: It names what is changed, what is measured and the conditions; the others have no measurable terms.

review.q: In a test of whether music affects recall, students in the music group are tested in the morning and the silent group after lunch. What is wrong?
choices: The dependent variable was never measured
There is no independent variable
Music cannot be an independent variable
Time of day is an uncontrolled variable that differs between groups
review.why: The groups differ in two ways at once, so any difference in recall cannot be attributed to the music alone.

review.q: What is the main purpose of a pilot study?
choices: To find problems in the procedure before the full experiment
To replace the need for a control group
To collect the final data faster
To convince the review board
review.why: A quick small run exposes practical problems while they are cheap to fix.

review.q: A student's data table has numbers but no units and several erased, rewritten entries. Why is this a problem?
choices: It uses too much paper
No one can tell what was actually measured or what the numbers mean
Erasing is against school rules
Tables must always be typed
review.why: Raw data must be recorded as observed and labeled with units, or the record cannot be checked or trusted.

review.q: Two groups differ in their means, but the ranges of values in each group overlap almost completely. What follows?
choices: The treatment worked
The larger mean is the true value
No real effect has been shown, since the difference is inside the scatter
The data should be deleted
review.why: A difference smaller than the spread within groups could arise by chance, so more evidence is needed.

review.q: What does the McClintock story show about scientific models?
choices: Models in genetics are useless
New evidence is always accepted immediately
A model is only as good as its record, and it is right to try to disprove it
A widely used model can be wrong outside the range where it was tested
review.why: The fixed-gene model worked for decades and then failed when McClintock's crosses tested it in a new situation.

review.q: Which of these is a criterion rather than a constraint for a footbridge?
choices: It must hold a load of 500 kilograms without visible bending
It must cost no more than the budget
It must be finished before the camp opens
It must not disturb the creek bed
review.why: A criterion describes measurable success; budget, deadline and protected creek bed are limits any design must obey.

review.q: A written explanation lists its own limitations and the alternative explanations it could not rule out. What effect should this have on a careful reader?
choices: It should make the reader reject the claim
It should increase trust, because the author has searched for weaknesses
It should be ignored as filler
It shows the author is unsure of everything
review.why: An explanation that honestly bounds itself shows the author is reporting what the evidence supports rather than selling a result.
